claims.text: The starting composite contains W particles or interconnected W ligaments embedded in a Cu matrix.
The W–Cu composite is prone to phase separation during processing and service.
The W–Cu composite is prone to interfacial void formation during processing and service.
A thin refractory ceramic or ceramic-like diffusion barrier can be deposited on W surfaces before composite consolidation.
A coating-derived interlayer promotes stronger interfacial cohesion.
The interlayer physically obstructs interdiffusion between W and Cu.
The barrier minimizes atomic interdiffusion and interfacial reactions.
Atomic interdiffusion and interfacial reactions cause phase demixing and void formation at W–Cu interfaces.
Suppressing interdiffusion and interfacial reactions maintains a coherent W–Cu microstructure.
Maintaining a coherent W–Cu microstructure facilitates efficient thermal conduction.
The barrier maintains this conduction-favorable microstructure under irradiation and thermal stress.
Barrier-coated W–Cu composites will have higher thermal conductivity than untreated W–Cu composites.
The barrier coating will reduce phase separation and interfacial void formation relative to untreated W–Cu composites.
The barrier coating will improve W–Cu microstructural stability under high heat flux and irradiation.
Untreated W–Cu composites exhibit significant phase separation and void formation at W–Cu interfaces under service conditions.
Interfacial phase separation and void formation reduce the thermal conductivity of untreated W–Cu composites.
The barrier is expected to remain effective under fusion-divertor-like thermal loads and irradiation.
Barrier efficacy may depend on achieving an optimal coating thickness and uniformity.
